subject: Civil Engineering
title: Punch Lists and Project Closeout
description: A short lesson to help you apply Punch Lists and Project Closeout.

hook.text: The building looks done — but 500 items need fixing. That list is the punch list.

buildup.text: The owner and architect walk every space — noting scratches, misaligned doors, and incomplete work.

discovery.text: Each punch item must be corrected before final payment — the contractor's incentive to finish right.

twist.text: Retainage — 5-10% of the contract held back — is released only after punch list completion.

climax.text: Closeout includes as-built drawings, warranties, and O&M manuals — the building's permanent record.

punchline.text: A project isn't done when it looks done. It's done when the last punch item is fixed.

quiz.question: What is retainage in construction contracts?
options: Extra materials kept on site for future repairs
A percentage of payment held back until punch list items are completed
The contractor's profit margin on the total project

details.summary: Project closeout encompasses punch list inspection of remaining defects, final testing and commissioning, as-built document compilation, warranty documentation, training of owner's maintenance staff, and financial closeout including final payment and retention release.
details.whyItMatters: Poor closeout leaves owners with incomplete documentation, unresolved defects, and no trained staff. It is the last impression and the beginning of the building's operational life.
takeaways: Punch lists document minor defects for correction before final acceptance
As-built drawings record actual construction conditions for future maintenance
Warranty periods typically begin at substantial completion or owner occupancy

faq.question: What is the difference between substantial completion and final completion?
faq.answer: Substantial completion occurs when the building can be used for its intended purpose even though minor punch list items remain. It typically triggers warranty periods and transfers risk to the owner.

faq.question: Why is project closeout often poorly executed in construction?
faq.answer: By closeout, key team members have moved to new projects, motivation to finish small items is low, subcontractors are reluctant to return for minor work, and attention shifts to new priorities.
